name: Brisbane
title: Brisbane UTM: Hull and Tank Thickness Gauging for Ships
description: Brisbane thickness gauging for tankers, bulk carriers, car carriers and container ships: ballast tanks, holds, decks and piping, alongside or at anchor.
h1: Thickness Measurement for Ships at the Port of Brisbane
intro: Brisbane's port sits at the mouth of the Brisbane River, mostly on reclaimed Fisherman Islands, and is reached through the long shipping channels of Moreton Bay. It handles container ships, car carriers, coal and grain bulkers, tankers serving the Lytton refinery and fuel terminals, and cruise ships at the river-mouth cruise terminal. Gauging here usually happens alongside during a cargo call or at an anchorage while a ship waits, and each job is staffed by technicians flown from India to the vessel; Atlantis keeps nobody in Queensland.

highlights.p: Container ships, car carriers and bulk carriers berth close together at Fisherman Islands near the river mouth. Their stays are usually long enough for a focused scope on deck plating, hatch coamings, ballast tanks or vehicle ramps, agreed in advance with the superintendent and timed to the cargo work.

highlights.h: Tankers at Lytton and the river wharves
highlights.p: Crude tankers call at the refinery's berth at Lytton, and product tankers discharge at the refinery products wharf and the common-user fuel berths. Ballast tanks, deck structure and cargo piping can be gauged during discharge; cargo tank entry depends on gas-freeing and the terminal's permits.

highlights.h: Waiting time turned into gauging time
highlights.p: Ships waiting for a berth, a grain stem or orders are held at the port's designated anchorages. Where the weather and the harbour master's rules allow, a launch arranged by the agent can put the team aboard, so days spent waiting become days of ballast tank and empty-hold measurement.

port.h: Moreton Bay, the river mouth and the Fisherman Islands terminals
p: The Port of Brisbane lies at the mouth of the Brisbane River on the western shore of Moreton Bay, a large, shallow bay sheltered from the Pacific by Moreton, North Stradbroke and Bribie islands. Deep-draught ships reach it through a long dredged channel system that runs from the open sea in the north down the length of the bay to the river entrance, a passage of several hours under compulsory pilotage. Maritime Safety Queensland runs the vessel traffic service and the harbour master's functions, while the port's land and berths are operated by the Port of Brisbane company under a long-term lease from the state. Most cargo berths are on Fisherman Islands, land reclaimed at the river mouth, with older wharves, fuel berths and the refinery further upstream.

Three container terminals on Fisherman Islands, run by DP World, Patrick and Brisbane Container Terminals, serve the deep-sea and feeder services from Asia, North America, Europe and the Pacific islands, and general cargo berths beside them take car carriers and ro-ro ships. Queensland Bulk Handling loads coal railed from mines west of the city at its terminal, GrainCorp ships grain, cottonseed and sugar, and other berths import fertiliser, cement clinker and dry bulk. The Lytton refinery, one of Australia's two remaining oil refineries, receives crude at its own berth and ships products from a separate wharf, and common-user berths at Luggage Point, Pinkenba and Fisherman Islands handle imported fuels. The Brisbane International Cruise Terminal near the river mouth lets the largest cruise ships berth without going far upriver.

Brisbane's subtropical climate shapes the work. The wet season, roughly December to March, brings heavy rain, thunderstorms and the occasional ex-tropical cyclone tracking down the coast, which can suspend open-deck work and launch transfers, and the river can flood after major rain in its catchment, bringing debris and strong currents into the lower reaches. The drier months from May to October are the easiest time for deck gauging and work at anchor. Deep-draught ships time their passage through the bay channels to the tide, which can move berthing times by several hours, and loaded bulk carriers in particular sail on the tide.

facilities.h: Gauging locations around the Port of Brisbane
p: Gauging in Brisbane is normally done alongside. The terminal operator at each Fisherman Islands berth sets the access rules, and the team works in the tanks and on deck around cargo operations, with an escort inside security zones for anyone who does not hold a Maritime Security Identification Card. At the refinery and fuel wharves, hot-work bans and permit systems apply, cargo tank entry needs gas-free certification, and the scope is usually limited to ballast tanks, deck structure and the cargo and ballast piping. Ships at a designated anchorage can be boarded by launch when the agent arranges it and the weather is suitable.

There is no working drydock for merchant ships in Brisbane at present. The historic Cairncross graving dock at Morningside, which once took ships of Panamax size, closed to commercial work in 2014, and in late 2025 the Queensland government declared a privately funded project to revive it as a working shipyard; until that is built, merchant ships trading to Brisbane dock in Asia. Slipways and boatyards along the river maintain tugs, pilot launches, dredgers, ferries and fishing vessels, and those craft can be gauged on the slip.
list: Fisherman Islands container terminals — deck plating, hatch coamings and scrubber piping on container ships during cargo work.
General cargo and motor vehicle berths — car carrier ramps, hoistable decks and ballast tanks while vehicles discharge.
Coal and grain terminals — hold, hopper and topside tank readings on bulk carriers, sequenced with loading.
Lytton refinery berths and common-user fuel wharves — crude and product tankers; ballast tanks, deck and cargo piping.
Brisbane International Cruise Terminal — cruise ships on turnaround; scrubber and void space pipework.
Designated anchorages — condition and pre-purchase gauging on waiting ships, boarded by launch.
River slipways and boatyards — tugs, dredgers, ferries and fishing vessels.

context.h: Queensland rules, AMSA and tanker vetting at Brisbane
p: Port state control at Brisbane is AMSA's responsibility, under Australia's membership of the Tokyo MoU and the Indian Ocean MoU, while Maritime Safety Queensland oversees pilotage, vessel traffic and the state's harbour rules. Brisbane is often a first or last Australian port for ships on the east coast, so it is frequently where an inspection happens soon after arrival. A ship that left an earlier port with hull or tank deficiencies to rectify does better with repair evidence and fresh readings on board when it arrives, and a short gauging scope during the call can provide both.

Tanker calls carry their own scrutiny. Crude and product tankers bound for the refinery and the fuel terminals are vetted by the receiving companies before they are accepted, and condition records, including recent thickness readings for ballast tanks and cargo piping, help an older tanker through that process. Every international arrival also has to report its biofouling management to the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry before entering Australian seas, a requirement in force since 15 June 2022, and ships that cannot show proactive management face further questions and a risk assessment. Biosecurity clearance must be in place before the team boards, which the agent confirms.

psc: Tokyo MoU and Indian Ocean MoU

jobs.h: What we are usually asked to gauge at Brisbane
jobs.p: Brisbane enquiries mix the port's trades. Tanker operators want ballast tank, deck and cargo piping readings for vetting and for planning the next docking; bulk carrier owners loading coal or grain want hold frames, hopper plating and topside tanks checked before charterer inspections or a sale; car carrier and container ship managers ask for ramp, deck and scrubber piping condition. With no commercial dock available, most work is owner's condition gauging, pre-purchase inspection or a steel estimate for a docking overseas. We set the scope with the superintendent against the expected berth time, allowing for tide and weather, mobilise the team from India once the visa is in hand, and deliver readings on the class formats with every location marked on the sketches.
list: Ballast tank and cargo piping gauging on a product tanker at a common-user fuel wharf, for the owner's vetting and maintenance records.
Hold frame, hopper and topside tank gauging on a Panamax bulk carrier loading coal at Fisherman Islands, ahead of a sale.
Pre-docking steel estimate for a container ship before its renewal survey in Asia.
Condition gauging of a car carrier's ballast tanks and lower vehicle decks during a long discharge call.
Hull gauging of a dredger or tug on a river slipway during maintenance.

logistics: Brisbane Airport is on the north bank of the river mouth and the port on the south bank, linked by the Gateway Motorway, so the team reaches the terminals by road. Indian nationals need an Australian visa for short-term specialist work, applied for once the call is firm, as processing times vary. The ship's agent arranges terminal access, security escorts and, for work at anchor, a launch, and confirms biosecurity clearance before boarding.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock in Brisbane?
faqs.a: Not one that takes merchant ships at present. The Cairncross graving dock at Morningside closed to commercial work in 2014, and a project to revive it as a working shipyard was declared by the Queensland government in late 2025 but has not yet been built. Ships trading to Brisbane therefore dock in Asia, and a Brisbane call is the place to gauge and prepare the yard specification.

faqs.q: Can bulk carriers be gauged while loading coal or grain?
faqs.a: Partly. Holds under the shiploader are off-limits, but holds that have not yet started loading can be entered early in the call, after the ship's own safety checks. Ballast, topside and hopper tanks are independent of the loading and can be measured once gas-tested, though the deballasting sequence decides when a given tank is empty enough to enter. We plan the order with the chief officer.

faqs.q: Does the wet season affect gauging plans?
faqs.a: It can. Between roughly December and March, thunderstorms and heavy rain stop work on open decks for periods, and an ex-tropical cyclone moving down the coast can close the port to shipping movements. Tank work continues in bad weather once the team is aboard. For deck-heavy scopes or work at anchor, the drier months from May to October are easier to plan.

faqs.q: Can a tanker's cargo tanks be gauged at the Lytton refinery berth?
faqs.a: Only if the ship can make the tanks gas-free and the terminal permits entry, which during discharge it normally will not. In practice, cargo tank gauging is done at anchor or in a yard, and a terminal call is used for ballast tanks, deck plating and the cargo and ballast piping on deck. We confirm the terminal's rules through the agent before the team travels.
